samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Dennis Hatzenbuehler was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Good morning.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Morning.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: My name is Robert Schmisseur and it's my pleasure this morningto be visiting with Mr. Dennis Dean Hatzenbuehler, who resides in Pratt, Kansas, at 613 West 2nd Street in Pratt, Kansas. This is part of the Veterans History Project. I'm cooperating with Tami Morse a Court Reporter who's a member of the National Court Reporters Association. Mr. Hatzenbuehler has been a friend of Tami's and mine for many years. He served as the bailiff for our Court here in Pratt, Kansas, for a number of years and became like family with us, and we are very proud to have the opportunity to record his history of service to our country for whatever uses the Library of Congress or researchers may have for this information in the future. Chief, how are you this morning?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: I'm fine. Thank you.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: You have filled out all the release forms and I think we're ready to get started. I think the best way to take a history is to go through chronological matters. Chief, why don't we talk about where you were born and your family life for a minute or two and then we'll get into your military service.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Well, I was born here in Pratt. My folks resided on a farm in Byers, Kansas, but I was brought in to go to school here at the Catholic school by my grandmother. So I stayed in Pratt here while the folks stayed out on the farm.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: And, Chief, why don't you talk about your folks and your grandparents. Somebody that might be looking at this tape 20 years from now would like their names because if they can tie it together for genealogical research and things like that, so who were your matter and father?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: My father was Leo and my mother was Teresa. Their grandparents -- well, I can't --

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Well, you made specific reference to your grandmother. Who was your grandmother that made sure you went to the Catholic school?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: That was my mother's mother.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: And what was her name?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Her name was -- I can't remember what her name was. Her last name was Sloan, Alpha Sloan. Yeah, Alfreda Sloan and so, ahh, she brought me into -- I went to school in Byers -- let me start. I went to school in Byers for the first year before I was six years old. My birthday is in January. I went to school in September the year before and that made me five. They kicked me out of school because I was too young, which generally in them days the farmers got to stay in school. But, anyway, I don't think they liked my father. But anyway, they -- so I had stayed out of school for a year so Grandma Sloan, my mother's mother, brought me in and I went to school there. So there I graduated.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: From the Catholic school here in Pratt?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: In the Catholic school in Pratt.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: That would be Sacred Heart Catholic School in Pratt?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: And from there on I went to, I graduated the 8th grade, went down to Pratt High School and I graduated out of there, so ...

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: And when did you graduate from high school, Chief?

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: After you finished high school in 1940 what was your first job out of high school?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Well, before high school I delivered the Pratt Tribune from '36 to '40, almost four years. And in 1938 or '39 I had a chance to go to CMTC that was a Citizens Military Training Camp. They paid me a dollar a day and I sent that home to mother and it was for four years basic, red, white and blue. So I went to basic, red -- and if I graduated out of that in four years I could become an officer in the Calvary, or the foot soldier. In 1940 they called me up and said, they cancelled everything. All the instructors are going east. At that time we was having a little conflict with the Germans and everything. So I decided, well, I'm going to join the Reserves. So I went to see my Catholic Priest Father Butler and so I went in the Navy. I joined the Reserves and in 1941, in July, they called me up. So that's how I got started in the Navy. I went to Great Lakes.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Great Lakes up in Illinois?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Illinois; and I think I was there for eight or twelve, weeks, I don't remember, and we took exams for physical and mentally, whatever they thought you should be into. And during high school I took typing, which I liked. I took shorthand for six months and I was the only boy, so I quit. But then in my resume I said, in their interview in Great Lakes that I had shorthand, and so that made me, which I shouldn't have done, but anyway when I got transferred they sent me to Corpus Christi, Texas. Before that I had a chance to go in aviation, or submarine duty and in submarine duty you have to be physically fit to get in submarines. But I turned them down, so I said, I'll go in aviation. So I went to Corpus Christi.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Chief, I want to stop you a second. When you were are called up to active duty in the Navy, we're talking at a time when the Germans have already invaded Poland. World War II is going on in Europe. The Japanese have invaded China. We weren't in the war yet, but at the point in time that you got called up in 1940, did you think the United States was going to fight in that war?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: No. No. I had no idea, you know. I was just a young kid running around here. We had no idea there was going to be a war. We just knew that there was a conflict and the only reason I knew it was because I was told that they took all our instructors and sent them east.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Now, your training officers, the noncommissioned officers and the commissioned officers that were your training officers, did they talk about things, like, you boys got to work hard and get ready because we're going to war or things of that nature?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Robert, all I know is the rugged exercise we had to go through, drills and that's all we did all day long for, I think, either eight or twelve weeks was -- well, with we had lectures, but I don't remember really what -- I had no idea there was going to be a war. I don't believe they ever said that. They just trained us to be what we were supposed to be and that was it.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: So when you finished your training at Great Lakes you went down to Corpus Christi, Texas?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Went to Corpus Christi, Texas, yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: And this was for what type of specific training down at Corpus Christi?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Well, when I got transferred to Corpus I went in the office as personnel because I had said I was a typist and I had shorthand. So that put me in an office and I really didn't want to, but that's where they sent me and during the office time why then that's how I got acquainted where I am today with my little lady.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Let's talk about your little lady a minute. How long you been married, Dennis?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: We're going on the 65th year.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: All right. And Phalba has been a friend of Tami's and mine for many years. Why don't you tell us a little bit about Phalba and how you met and I know her father was a distinguished -- had a distinguished and Naval career. Just tie him in a little bit, because somebody doing research may want to cross reference some of this.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Okay. I went to the personnel office and there was three ladies, three working in there. And so I joined them and we became real good friends and this one young lady I kind of liked, but I couldn't touch her, because sitting over there in the desk was the personnel officer and he was quite a wheel and that was his daughter and, you know, I knew right off the bat I couldn't mess with that. That was for sure. So anyway I got what I wanted as time went by. I wanted to buy a set of blues, right, a set of blues?

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: And then I -- in them days the old uniforms was like these and I wanted bell-bottoms. I wanted to be a wheel and my cuffs had dragons and I really wanted to be a wheel, see. So I saved my money. I think I had a hundred dollars.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: And so one day I just asked Phalba, you know, I want to get a new set of blues and you've been around a long time, all your life. Would you pick me out a pair? And she said, "Sure." So we went to Corpus Christi and we're walking down the street and I don't remember the jewelers.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Past a jewelry store.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: What was the name? I don't remember. Anyway, we passed a jewelry store and saw all them rings and everything. And we just sat and looked and I said, "Boy there's, you know" --

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: You asked me, you said, "Which ring do you like?"

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Yeah. Then I said, "Well, let's go inside and you just look. Try one on." So we found one she liked and I said, "Do you want this?" And she said, "Yes." That was it. Never asked her to get married. Nothing. I just said, "Do you want this ring?" She said, "Yes". So anyway she -- we knew we was going to be in problems.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay; and we've talked about Phalba and that you folks worked together and obviously you took a real shine to her and she took a real shine to you.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: I don't know about that, but I took a shine to her.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: I thought he was cute, but that's it.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: If she was willing to take a ring from you she was taking a shine to you, fella. Don't underestimate that. You mentioned her dad worked there in the office. Your father-in-law what was his name?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Ralph.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Christensen?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Christian.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: And I've seen pictures of him here at your home and I know you've talked about him with, with great respect. Let's just tie in a little bit of his Naval career and then we'll get back on to your's.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: He went in the Navy pretty young.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: He went in when he was 19.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: 19-years old he went to the Navy and this time he was stationed in Annapolis and the five.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Tell him how he started.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: He went to Annapolis and to make it short he taught the cadets how to fly and he didn't know how to fly. They figured out, and I guess he done something, and they sent him to Pensacola.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: No, he went to Pensacola first.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Well, okay.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: And he got his wings and he was a First Class AP, which was very unusual.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Phalba, what did AP stand for?

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Aviation pilot.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: And he met my mother down there and he went -- we went to San Diego from there and he, he was, he was a first class pilot.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. And we've been chatting a little bit here with Phalba Hatzenbuehler, Dennis' better half of 65 years now. Phalba, just why don't you give us the 90 second version of your father's career, his ranks and ...

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Okay. He started out as a First Class AP and he made Chief. He made Warrant Lieutenant, JAG Lieutenant and then Lieutenant Commander. He retired as a Lieutenant Commander.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: And a couple of the ships he served, I know he was on the carriers?

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Well, he was on the Intrepid, but he was in a squadron stationed at North Island and they flew, took the squadron to the carriers. The Enterprise, the old Enterprise, the old Saratoga. He was one of the first pilots that landed on the Langley and then he was on the Wright.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. When you said North Island you mean in Hawaii they would shuttle the planes from Hawaii out to the carriers?

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: No from San Diego, California.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: And they go out and land on the carriers and they go out to sea with the carriers. That's where they get the maneuvers and whatnot. Right?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Yeah, right, dear.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay; and since we're talking a little bit about your father-in-law, Dennis, you have related a story to me a time or two of when you and he were on the same ship during World War II and since we're talking about him right now, let's put that story and record it for history.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Well, before I get to that, see, he was going to transfer me.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. Yeah. When you're -- when his daughter had your ring on he didn't approve?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: He didn't approve. So he transferred me to Kingsville, Texas and so I was down there, back and forth, and back, and all of a sudden I got a phone call, one of the girls in the office says, "Dennis, you're getting transferred. Do you and Phalba want to get married?" I said, "Sure. How about her?" She said, "Yeah, she's ready." So we got married. Well, then we came back -- he brought me back to Corpus after that, but then I knew I was going to get transferred. Well, I did. I got transferred and that's all in here. So that's how all that started.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. You got transferred from Corpus Christi, to where?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Well, if I may.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Livermore, didn't you?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: "Naval Recruiting Station, Kansas City, Missouri; Naval Air Training Center, Great Lakes, Illinois; Naval Air Station, Corpus Christi, Texas; Naval Air Station, Kingsville, Texas; ABATU, Naval Air Station, Norfolk, Virginia. That was when I was going aboard the Intrepid. Norfolk, Virginia; Carrier Aircraft Service Unit 6, Alameda, California; USS Intrepid (CV-11); Aircraft Carrier Service Unit 5, San Diego, California; Naval Air Station, Quonset Point, Rhode Island; Patrol Squadron 62, Naval Air Station, Patuxent River, Maryland, B24s; Miramar, California; Naval Air Station, Hutchinson, Kansas; P2Vs; Patrol Squadron 22, Honolulu, Hawaii; Naval Air Facility, China Lake, California; Airborne Early Warning Squadron 3, Naval Air Station, Guam; Patrol Squadron 42, Navy Air Station, North Island, San Diego, California; Patrol Squadron 31, Naval Air Station, Whidbey Island, Washington; Naval Air Station, Olathe, Kansas; and then to Training Squadron 27, Naval Air Station, Corpus Christi, Texas. There is where I retired. Now, I don't have anything in here about all the time I was in Vietnam or nothing. They didn't put that in there.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: They were in Miramar. You got alot of North Island on there.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Yeah, alot of stuff out.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Well, they had several million people to keep track of records on and some of it apparently slipped through the cracks. But anyway you and Phalba got married on a sly?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Yep.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: And I assume that her dad didn't really like that?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: No, he didn't.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: And at that point in time what would his rank have been?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: He was Lieutenant.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. So I assume that in the Navy a Lieutenant kind of got his way with the enlisted personnel?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: He was the boss.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. So when he found out you married his daughter, what, he transferred you to --

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: East Coast that's when I started all that stuff.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: And, Phalba, did you stay then at home or did you follow this guy around?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: She stayed in Corpus Christi, and then come to Pratt.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: I came here in '44.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. So we're talking -- Chief, let's talk about December 7th, 1941. Where were you and when did you find out that you were in a war?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: We were at Corpus.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: We were at Corpus Christi and I think I was going out -- it was on a Sunday morning. Now, you have to realize we had duty station, then. We had four duty stations in the Navy, then. Three-quarters of it was on shore, a quarter had to stay a board all the time. My duty station that day, I got off, I think I was heading to town or something. I can't remember where I was headed. The marine stopped me at the gate and said, "Get back to your base as soon as possible." Wouldn't tell me why. So in Corpus Christi, now that was just a new base. The runways were there. The barracks were there. But no sidewalks, mud. It was pathetic. But anyway, we got back out to the hangar and here a great big old B-24 come taxing up. Well, we didn't know what was going on and all of a sudden then they put lines out around that. We couldn't -- then we found out that it was a war. That was how we found out. That simple.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: All right. And what was your first duty assignment then after we were at war with Japan and war with Germany? What was your first duty assignment? You were at Corpus Christi?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: I was in the office. Then I found out that to make Second Class -- I made Third Class, but to make Second I had to know shorthand because that's how they did it in them days. The old man when he'd talk to you it was shorthand. You had to write shorthand. So I went down and worked on the hangar deck and changed my rate to MEC and I made Second Class real fast like. So I could have -- Second Class they got their rations and money for rent and stuff. So I was, let me see, I can't remember. I flew -- we had two APs. We had a First Class AP and a Second Class AP and we had the yellow N2Ns, N2S's bi-wing and we put instruments in it for weather. That's how we go up and fly and so I would fly with them until I got transferred.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. And so the planes that they had down there at Corpus Christi were for pilots to learn how to fly?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Learn how to fly, yes.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. So they were -- you rattled off a couple of buzz numbers and words that would mean something to the folks that had studied this, but why don't you talk about those airplanes just a little bit more. Are they one seaters, two seaters?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: They were two seaters, little yellow pearls, and they had wings and they had cross-sections on them, that's where we'd put the instruments for the weather and the APs flew them and then we took care of them out on the flight line. I was in charge of the flight line and, because I was Second Class, and so I get to fly with them and that's about it.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. So you got involved in the maintenance aspect --

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: -- of aircraft very early in your Naval carrier?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: And then when you left Corpus what was your next duty assignment?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: When I left Corpus I think I went to ABATU in Norfolk, Virginia.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. What does ABATU stand for?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: I have no idea what it stands for.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. But --

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: It's a training, aviation training unit.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Well, ABATU, I can't remember what it was.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. But it was -- you would have continued in your training on aircraft maintenance?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Oh, ABATU, we made engines for all the aircraft and I was an inspector and when the engine would come to be final, to be put out the door, I had to inspect it. I had certain things to do to make sure that everything was perfect and that was, that was that.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. At this point in time all the airplanes would have been propeller airplanes. You wouldn't have had any jets --

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: -- in service and the, you know, when we think of Navy aviation we think of aircraft carriers, but it sounds like the pilots and the maintenance crews, et cetera, would have done a great deal of work long before they were ever going to get on an aircraft carrier?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Oh, Lord, yes.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: So where you at were there in Virginia was basically -- basically we're getting ready to fight a war and, of course, we already are fighting a war and getting our butts kicked out in the Pacific and the United States is getting ready to build the war machine that was necessary to win both in Europe and Japan or in the Pacific. So we're basically getting that war machine ready to go?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: And how many hours a day were you working on an average day when you were there in Virginia?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Oh, we'd go to work -- we'd have to be to work by 8:00 o'clock and maybe it would be 7:00, 8:00, 9:00 o'clock at night before I got out. We had the engines in a row there that had to be inspected to get out underway and so until the last one -- the civilians built the airplanes and the Navy we got -- we had to inspect it. In other words, big old great engines there and you had a crank and you had to turn it and listen to this sound and see if everything is -- and it was your own ability to say that plane's ready to go, or that engine's not ready to go and another one would come in and it would be maybe 10 hours, 12 hours.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: And approximately how long were you there in Virginia?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: I was there -- the Intrepid left and then they shipped me across and I picked up the Intrepid in Frisco.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay; and the Intrepid was a CV-11?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: CV-11, yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: And at that point in time that would have been as hot of a carrier as we had?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: CV the biggest.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: And of course the Intrepid has been docked in New York City. I think it's actually back over in New Jersey getting refurbished right now. I had the opportunity, a year or so ago Donna and Joe and I spent a half a day on the Intrepid and it was very meaningful to us knowing that you'd served there and it was -- I didn't find a bunk that said "Hatzenbuehler" next to it, but you joined the Intrepid in San Francisco and this would have been approximately 1942?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: No. No. No. That was after, after '43 I got transferred to Norfolk and it was --

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: -- it was sometime right after that. I wasn't there very -- I wasn't at Norfolk more than six months I don't think.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: So in 1943 you went on board the Intrepid?

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: I think it was first part of '44 I went aboard the Intrepid.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: First part of '44 up went on board of the Intrepid and was your father-in-law on board of the Intrepid at that time, too?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. How was it having your father-in-law on the same ship?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Well, I'll tell you a little story. When I went aboard, of course, we carried our sea bag and our hammock. Anyway when you go aboard you salute and the officer of the deck says -- when I said, "Hatzenbuehler reporting." Why he says, by the way you're to report to, or somewhere, and I knew exactly what he meant. I said, "Well, okay." I said, "I'm tired. I want to get rid of this stuff I have here. And I'll report to him." Well, I didn't do it. I didn't go and I just forgot about it. Well, anyway we went on a shakedown and had a little problem. Anyway we headed for Honolulu and I'm up on the hanger deck, flight deck -- no, I'm on the hangar deck. I'm going forward and the doors are open on the starboard side and there's a full Lieutenant Commander standing there and I knew who it was. So I went and tapped him on the shoulder and he kind of got a little upset because I didn't report to him. Anyway to be truthful to you nobody in the -- now to get things -- he was, he was probably the air officer aboard and he was strict, I mean, he was awful strict. Oh, but anyway I, I -- we talked and outside of that, that was fine. We were okay.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Let's talk just a little bit, you mentioned an air officer. An aircraft carrier is kind of a unique Naval vessel in that there's the, there's the folks that make sure that the ship gets from where it needs to go to where it needs to go. And then there's also basically an airport that's there and there's all the airplanes and there's the folks that worry about the airplanes and there's the folks that worry about the ship. Let's --

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: He worried about the airplanes, getting the airplanes airborne and getting them aboard that was it and he'd walk the decks at night seeing us guys are working because you had to have a hundred percent. They wanted a hundred percent every morning, but that was almost impossible.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: So your father-in-law would have been the Lieutenant Commander and he would have been basically the air officer?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: He was Assistant Air Officer, I think.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: The Assistant Air Officer on the Intrepid? Who was the commanding officer on the Intrepid at that point in time do you remember?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: I have no idea, no.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: What type of rank would --

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: He was a Captain, four striper.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Now, he -- our skipper went to the -- in 1944-45 he got transferred and he went to another, they just built a great big carrier, a larger carrier than the Intrepid, larger than the CV. I can't remember what it was. He went aboard of that to take over as the skipper.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: When you're getting shook down, you're getting ready to go into combat, what types of airplanes would you have had; how many; that sort of thing.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Well, I was, I was assigned to the SP2C we had 15 --

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. And a SP2C was a torpedo plane?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Torpedo plane and then we had the TBM or SBC or SP2C, TBM and that was a torpedo. I think the SP2-Cs was a bomber type. We dropped the bomb, but the torpedo was a TBM.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. So your main deal was a torpedo plane or was a dive bomber?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: We were a dive bomber, really.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. And so you'd had had some torpedo planes and you'd have had some dive bombers and would you had had some fighters on board, also?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: We would have 50, 60 fighters, maybe not quite that many, but I know the aircraft was full of planes.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. What type of fighters would you have been carrying at that point in time?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: We were carrying at first the F-4.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: The Hell Cats?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Then we went to the F-6.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: The Corsair?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: The F-6. Then we went to the F-4a, the Corsair.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: That was a nice plane. Then at the end of the war we got the, we had the F-6. Then we got the F-8. That was, that was supposed to be the one time jobber, no maintenance or nothing, just made one hop and then you deep-six it. But it didn't pan out that way. They were our night fighters. They were a little fast, little jewel. Little smaller than the other. The father of the outfits. They were pretty good.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: As a practical matter, Tami, we're going to loose that battery long before we get done here. So, basically, your carrier would have had some torpedo planes and some dive bombers and some fighters and the basic purpose was to fight Japanese ships rather than to support land operations?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: To fight. We didn't, we didn't, we were no land support. We were just strictly dog fighting.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: What was the first operation that you recall where the Intrepid would have been involved in a fight with the Japanese?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Oh, Lord, we no more than got out there when we left Frisco and we were -- well, let's see, your daddy took two crash dives and they come into port. Then we went back out we took, I think, three or four more -- three more crash drives.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. Approximately where in the Pacific are we talking about that you took those Kamikazes?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: I don't know. They were around Guam, somewhere around in that area. I have no idea where we were at.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Where was the Franklin?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Well, she was out there, too, that was later on.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Well, you guys were out there with the Franklin at one time.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Yeah, but we were about 15 miles from her when she got hit.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: So the plane, the ship took significant damage when it took those Kamikazes?Dennis Hatzenbuehler:: Yes.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: And you went back to port and got refitted, and I'm assuming that some of the personnel would have got transferred other places and your planes would have went somewhere else and you got restocked, then, when the ship was ready to go back out?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Yes. Yes.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Do you remember when -- are we into 1945, when the ship went back out, or are we still in '44?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: I think in '44. When we got hit 45.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: That's when you --

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: January in '45 I think we were in Hunters Point, because I come back and picked mother up and we went back out.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: And Hunters Point is in California?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Yes, in California dry dock.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: San Francisco.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: We then went back out and I think in January we took a hit, February or March, somewhere in there the Franklin got hit and then we took another hit and then we went into a repair ship somewhere out there instead of coming back to dry dock, we, we went to a repair ship and went there for three or four weeks getting fixed up. We had a pretty good size hole in our flight deck and so then, well, then the war was over with.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: And how many Kamikazes did the Intrepid take while you were on deck or while you were on board?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Three. Three.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. And this was probably off Okinawa?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: I think it was Okinawa, yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Okinawa.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Where were you when the first Kamikaze hit?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: When the first Kamikaze hit I was in -- I don't remember where I was at. I don't remember where I was at.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. I mean, you were at general stations of some type?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. So you were on stations and I know from having toured the Intrepid that it got the living hell tore out of it and there was a real question whether or not the ship was going to make it or not. I'd like to talk for a couple of minutes about what it was like to take a Kamikaze like that and what the ship was doing and what you were doing to try to keep afloat.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: You was up by the fo'c's'le --

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Fo'c's'le.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: -- yeah, that one time.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Yeah. Well, Robert, I'll tell you things happen so fast that you don't worry about nothing. You just worry about yourself. If you can help somebody -- I remember up on the fo'c's'le when we, the -- one of the ships was up on our port bow and they were strafing and I and my First Class were, we were standing together and we'd just come from the mess hall when the general quarters sounded. There was a few of us at general quarters. I hate to say it, but we didn't have no duty station. We could do whatever we wanted. There was three or four of us could do whatever we wanted. So -- I was one of them. I had no duty station. I could do whatever I wanted. We went to the fo'c's'le and the plane was strafing and I had a sandwich in my hand. General quarters sounded when I was down in the third, second deck or wherever the mess hall was and I dropped my sandwich and I reached down to pick it up and Chesner was over here. Somehow Chesner got his arm shot off. Well, he fell down on me. Well, anyway we got him squared away, wrapped him in a canvas.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Is that where you took the ankle?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Oh, yeah, well, that was a different story. That was -- the funny part of it was I had a big cast on. See, when we come into port I figured I'd get transferred. I was right on that ship. So I was it -- this is I got to go down and light the burners for chow and start the stoves about 4:00 o'clock in the morning, light the stoves, but outside of that, that was nothing.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Well, you've told me a story in the past that I think is important to commemorate. There was a anti-aircraft crew on the Intrepid that received quite a bit of notoriety and as I recall the story your father-in-law, and maybe I'm not remembering the story right, wasn't very happy with those guys that they didn't have their proper equipment on and --

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Their flash gear.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Yeah. They didn't have their flash gear on.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: And what's flash gear?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Well, that's a -- it's burn -- it won't burn or anything and you put it over your head. You put gloves on, come all the way up and you've got to have your sleeves and everything down, so you're really covered, if you get a flash burn it's not going to hurt you because this stuff will --

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Places over your nose and mouth.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Anyway these guys didn't have their flash gear on. Well, when a Betty or something was coming on the starboard side, because I was on the port and I was on the catwalk, I was up on the flight deck watching that sucker and the guns were going off and anyway it exploded and all that crap came aboard, all the shrapnel, everything came aboard and kids got hurt. The old man took them all down and put them in a row before they even got fixed up and took pictures of them --

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Regulation.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: -- and put them on report.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: And as I recall these, these sailors were black, weren't they?

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Yep. They were all colored.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: What, what was -- and in 1944, 1945 what was the segregation circumstances on the carrier? Were the blacks in the same crew quarters as the whites?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. We got along good.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Just some of them try to pull a little, you know, if you, my mother or so will write the Congressmen if you do so and so. People like that during the war and most of them there was alot of black. There was some white's, too, but there was alot of blacks and they caused alot of trouble at that time.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: At that time I didn't know what segregation was. We didn't have that around Pratt here. I played football. I played with the colored boy down south. I knew they couldn't get up too far in town here. We rode on busses with them, so we didn't know anything about --

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Well --

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: -- segregation when I got out to sea.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: I know the suggestion was in the Army that black soldiers generally did not get involved in the frontline combat units. They were involved in matters of supply and they worked as truck drivers and stevedores and things like that. They weren't on the frontline combat units. But on the ship you had, as we've described before, really a ship is just a big city. It's got to have everything that you need to take care of potentially several thousand people, plus fight. So that there is no frontline in the Navy?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: You know, on the beach you got 500 people. You got 12 airplanes. Everything goes smooth. You get out to sea with them 12 airplanes you may only took -- like us mecs on the beach, we'd have 25, 30. But when I went on the carrier maybe only four or five of us. So that -- but, anyway, the colored people aboard, I remember, I remember the colored boys on the port, fantail they're the ones that got the hit that was notarized in the papers and everything. That turret really got it and they just -- as them Kamikazes were coming in they stayed in battle stations or didn't budge. One guy they said did and they were going to court martial him, but -- and I don't think they did. I don't remember, but we didn't pay no attention to that.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: That was just regulation.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: We didn't have time to do that. We had to get airplanes airborne. We didn't have time -- I never -- I never went down and had coffee and smoked a cigarette because I didn't smoke. I stayed on that engine up on the hangar deck.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Your whole Navy life was like that. You never sat and had coffee with the guys.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. Well, you talked -- you were on the Intrepid and the historian can certainly go take a look at the Intrepid's records and pin everything together as to what we're talking about. You said, the war was over.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: What made you decide that, I'm going to stay in the Navy rather than get out when the war was over?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Well, let me see, 1949, see I shipped over so my enlistment wasn't right. Anyway, when the war was over they sent us to the Yellow Sea, Halsey sent us to the Yellow Sea and we were up in the Yellow Sea an order from Maypack come aboard, if you hadn't had any leave, or I guess if you hadn't had any leave, get out. So, boy, I didn't have no leave during the war. Man, I hitchhiked all the way back, and this was about September, I hitchhiked all the way back in different ships and stuff and mother was in Kingman. I opened the door in Kingman on Thanksgiving day. I opened it and it was 25th of November.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: 1945, yeah. And so then I was -- I had orders to go to flight school. I was going to go to flight school and I had 64 days leave, I think, and during that time I got orders flight school has been cancelled. You're going to go back to sea, some carrier at North Island. So, man, here I go and I got to North Island. Get the family out there. An order comes out and again says if I had nothing, something to do, I can't remember what it was now, oh, shore duty. I hadn't done no shore duty. I was at sea. They gave me three places to go I picked Quonset Point, Rhode Island. So that's how I got to Rhode Island, Quonset Point was B-24s. That was my life, B-24s.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Now, for somebody like me that knows just enough about military stuff to be dangerous, I think of a B-24 as a big, heavy, four-engine bomber that we would have used to bomb the heck out of the Germans and that sort of thing. What in the world is the Navy doing with a B-24? You couldn't land that B-24 on a carrier?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: We were photographing for the State department. That's how we took our pictures. Our pictures were taken at 29,000, I think 29 and a half thousand feet. We had radio altimeters to let us know how high we were so that's what we did there.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: He was in they photographic squadron then.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: You're in a photographic squadron, that was a Navy squadron. You're flying the heavy, four-engine bombers that they've put special equipment in for photography?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Yeah. We took all the heavy armor stuff out that they had during the war and like, especially, over on the east. So we were, we were equipped with big oxygen tanks because you flew at 29,000 feet three and four hours, you know. To photograph we take off at 6:00 o'clock or 7:00 and it was a pretty slow airplane. So by the time we got to 29,000 feet may have been a couple of hours. Then at sunset you can photograph and then about 3:00 o'clock in the afternoon you can't photograph any more. So then it takes you a couple more hours to get down.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: You said sunset. You can photograph when the sun is high in the sky?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Yes, no clouds.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: So, basically, late morning to early afternoon is a window of time to photograph?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Only about four or five hours in there that you could photograph.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay; and I know you've talked about being in the Middle East and I remember you've talked about being down in South America. Where were some of the places that you would have photographed with that unit? I know you were up in Goose Bay, Labrador. Where were some of the places that you would have went with that photograph unit?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Without?

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: No with the, with that unit in the B-24s and I know you've talked about the Connies, too, but was the Connie a photograph one also?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: No. No.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Let's talk about the B-24 and the photographs. Where around the world did you go to take those pictures?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Well, okay, I started out -- okay, when I got my orders out of Quonset Point to B-24s was New Jersey. Well, I'm home here in Pratt. I get orders that New Jersey, they're moving to Patuxent River, Maryland. So then I went to Patuxent River and the first week I was there we were headed for St. Johns, headed for Goose Bay St. Johns.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Up in Canada?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Up in Canada. So we went up there and we left here in May. Yeah, we left here in May. We photographed St. Johns for awhile until the snow melted up in Goose Bay, Labrador. We had to be back in September.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: So at that point in time you're photographing up in Canada?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: We was photographing up in Canada, yeah, everything. I don't know why, but we were photographing. We were back here in September. We had to be in Arabia the end of September because you can only photograph there, the sun -- there's no clouds or nothing and so we photographed there until December.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Well, we got transferred. You went there and then we had to go back to San Diego.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Well, I went to Goose Bay, Labrador, I mean to Arabia. Came back to Patuxent River. We get back in December from Goose Bay, from Arabia. Then we had to be in South America in January, the first. So we only had a short span to get your airplanes fixed up, because it was my airplane that we was flying, or I was the plane Captain of it. Then we go to South America. We'd be stationed at Panama and then we had to go down to Medellin. All them countries down there and photograph. And we photographed until they started burning the fields, cane and stuff and that was in May. So then we'd come back her Alameda.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: California?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: California and this was in May. Okay. It would be the first of May. The end of May, I'm headed back for St. Johns, Goose Bay, Labrador, Arabia, back here, back to South America. Come back here. And I done that three or four times. And then, you know, it was time for me to get -- they said, you're going to get sea duty. You've got to go to sea duty now and they -- classified this as preferred sea duty. Well, anyway I had a friend in the bureau that I got me wherever I wanted to go and --

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: That was your father-in-law?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: No. No. It was a good friend of mine.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Is it okay to mention his name?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: No, I don't think -- remember their names. Anyway, I called him up and I said -- after I got back from South America, they called me up and said, "Get your plane ready. The crew in Italy's passports are expiring and you just got a new passport." And I said, "Hey, wait a minute. I just got back and I haven't been with these people for three -- two and a half years." So I got on the phone and I talked to my boy up there and he said, "Okay". So I went up and told the -- Commander Connan was going to go back with us and he -- we kind of got along pretty good. He had a half a dozen, six, eight, nine kids and I had six and we had all our -- we had all the faces painted on the bow of our, my plane. I think we had 16 or 18 baby faces up there and that was how many kids we had. But anyway I went up to see Connan and I said, "I got my orders to get transferred, Commander." And he says, "Oh, I'm not signing them." He says, "You're going with me. We're going back to Italy." And I said, "Oh, come on." And I went home and I told momma, "I guess, we're shot down again." So the next day I'm going to go back and talk to Connan. Well, he wasn't in his office and I said, "Where's he at?" He said, "Well, he's got the day off." And I said, "Oh." The assistant and he says so and so, and so I went and saw the assistant so he said, "Sure, I'll sign them." So off I went, boy, I went to Hutchinson, Kansas. I sure did. I went to Hutchinson.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: The first time.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: The first time, yeah. I got the heck out of there, man.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. Now, Hutchinson, Kansas is right in the center of the United States. What in the world was the Navy doing with a station in Hutchinson, Kansas?

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Reserves.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: No. We were -- this was where they were training pilots for the squadrons out at sea, the P2Vs. We had the SB22s are the ones, the first ones that came out and that's what we were doing there.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: So that was a training squadron.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Here in Pratt we had the B-29 base up north of town and there was a Naval Air Station at Hutchinson that was developed during World War II to make sure that, you know, that we could train the personnel to go fight the war and as we commented earlier you don't fly off the carrier in the beginning. You got to learn how to fly first and then you learn to fly off the carrier.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: That's right. That's what we did at Hutch.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: The base up at Hutchinson was to train pilots so that ultimately they could serve in combat or support roles on the front lines in the Navy?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Very well.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: And approximately -- you said you got into Hutchinson, can you tell me approximately what year that would have been?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: '52, '52, yeah, sometime in the middle of '52.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: All right. And how long did you stay in Hutchinson?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Ahh, I got my orders in '55 and --

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: And during this time you'd have been in Hutchinson you'd have still been involved in aircraft maintenance?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Well, I was plane Captain of about every recip they had on the -- I was qualified to fly in all the recips we had on the ships.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: And when you say a recip, what's a recip?

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Prop

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: That's the propeller airplane.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. And what rank would you have had in the service at that point?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: I was First Class then.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. So you spent about three, three and a half years in Hutchinson?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: And, basicaly, it was your job to make sure that when the pilots wanted to go out and fly they had an airplane that would take them up and bring them back?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: That's exactly right.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: And when you got done with your duty in Hutchinson where'd you go?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Okay. I got my orders to go back to sea.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: In '55? We went to Hawaii.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: I got my orders in Hutchinson, 1955. So I get on the phone, called my boy up and I said -- come home and asked momma, "Do you want to go to Honolulu?" She said, "Sure." I said, "Okay, let's go." I called the joker up and he said, "You'll have orders to Honolulu."

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Second time.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Mother had been out there before the war.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: I went to school out there.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: So I just thought it would be nice to get her back out there. When she was there, there was no cement on --

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Oh, man, this was pretty.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: No cement at all. When I came back in -- coming back in '44 or '45 nothing but cement, you know, none of the pretty flowers. All the dirt was gone.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: And then Kaiser moved in and took over.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: But anyway that's how I got to Honolulu and BP-22. Right there I got me an aircraft. I was there two days. The ship hadn't got our cars there, hadn't got our furniture there, hadn't got nothing there, and I'm headed for Guam or --

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: We had no furniture or nothing.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: I was heading for somewhere, anyway. So mother was there and had -- I bought a little old -- so many people moving and going and moving and going that I just picked up a old Plymouth for, I don't know, I have no idea what I paid for it. But that was Momma's car until ours came aboard. Now, I'd just bought a brand new 1955 Chevy station wagon. I got it at Haven, nice one. And so now I'm taking that sucker to Honolulu for salt water and stuff, but anyway that's how I got to ...

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: So you got to Honolulu, but you got there a couple of days and the family gets left behind and you're off to Guam?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: I think I went to Guam or somewhere. I can't remember. It was about four or five --

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: You went to Guam one time because we couldn't --

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: That was later on, Doll Baby. Either at Sucki, Okinawa, there were four or five different bases, two up in Japan, Taiwan. Anyway, I don't remember where all we went.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: So at this stage of your career you're not on the carriers. You're being basically Naval air station that are on land and you're still working as a mechanic. You're supervising other mechanics basically at that point in time?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: But you're the one that's got to sign off whether that airplane is ready -- Dennis Hatzenbuehler:: Ready to go.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: -- is ready for service or not?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Right now.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: What type of pressures do you get from folks higher up the chain of command to make sure that those airplanes are ready to go or if the, if the flight commander is saying, "I want, I want a hundred percent of the birds in the air tomorrow." What do you have to do to make sure you got a hundred percent of the birds in the air?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: When you're boss up there in Kingman tells you you got to do this and that, you do it. That's exactly what I had to do. I mean, I want a hundred airplanes in the morning, or I want a hundred percent. I want 150, you can't give a hundred percent, but you've got to try. And the old man, the Skipper's lenient to that, but he wants to know why, by-cracky why, and who. Haven't you gotten the right kind of men? You know, you got to -- if you want to keep your rate, you know, and I certainly didn't want to -- I had how many kids to feed.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Well, Chief, let's talk about what it takes to keep an airplane in the air. You know, most of us think about an automobile that basically all we do is put a little gas in the tank and every 2500 or 3000 miles, you know, we change the oil every three, four, 5000 miles and alot of automobiles any more will go a 100,000 without having any type of significant work other than putting some tires on it and changing the oil and a battery and pretty simple things. What kind of work do you have to do to keep an airplane in the air and, basically, we're talking about some of those planes that you had during World War II. How many hours could they fly before you were going to have to do a major overhaul on them?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Well, let's just say I'm landing, we're coming in for a landing and we're retiring for the evening. We pull what you called a post-flight. In other words, my crew took all the (cowlings) off of the B-24, every night, every time come in from a flight, check all oil leaks, and then you had so many hours, every 30 hours, you had to check/pull. That means go through everything. Complete overhaul every 30 hours. Then at 60 hours you had another complete check, but it was a little bit different. It included more stuff that had to be done. A 120 hours check you had to pull the prop off. Maybe had to take the carburetor off. You had a whole lot of work to do. That's what you done. Now, before I went off in the morning if I had a 7:00 o'clock flight I had to be there at 5:00 o'clock, 5:30. Pull what you call a preflight check. Check everything again, (cowling) comes off, check for oil leaks during the night. Oil in them big engines seems to seep down into the bottom of the jugs. Well, if you got in the airplane and hit your starter and that piston hit that oil it grounds down in that piston with them two valves closed you had a bent rod. So you had to pull all your blades through by hand to get the oil moving and that's what it contained and it took you a couple -- took a good hour and a half to get that plane ready for flight.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: So basically you would have had a schedule on that airplane that says after so many hours we're going to do this?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: After so many hours we're going to do that. Let's say that that plane comes back into the carrier and the pilot says, "I felt this vibration." Or, "I thought I had this problem."

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: You got to fix it.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. And you're in the combat zone and you need to get that airplane back in the air as quick as you can to keep you alive and to keep everybody else alive. So there were times that you'd work all night to get that airplane ready again?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: On the carrier?

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: We work 24 hours a day, seven days a week, four weeks a month. We never got no time off. I took a fresh water shower aboard that aircraft, aboard the carrier, I might have taken one. I go back -- I might have taken one fresh water shower. The rest of them, saltwater showers, maybe twice a week and them old saltwater showers with that saltwater soap, buddy, is no fun. But that fresh water shower they had a coxian maid or you got a minute 30 seconds wash down, water goes off, because you can only get so much fresh water aboard that ship and you got, what, all them people aboard. So that was it. Salt water you could stay all day long. Who wanted to stay in that salt water all day long.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Vietnam when he was in the reserves --

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Oh, well, yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: We haven't quite got that far yet.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: So you were, late '50s, you're out in the --

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: '55 I'm in Honolulu and them places.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Then you're hitting those duty stations in Japan and Taiwan and places like that. Your wife mentioned Viet Nam. The United States was involved in the Vietnam War for, what, some 12, 13 years something like that, from the mid-60s and I think it was 1975 when Saigon fell. What type of duty work did you do in Vietnam?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Same thing.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: You were on a carrier or on shore?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Well, on shore, shore duty.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. And where in Vietnam were you stationed?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Okay. First I went to Cameron Bay -- no. No. When I went to -- okay we're going back -- we're going to VP. We're going to VP-1 now.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: A VP was a one time airplane?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: We had the latest PTV, the P2s, jet engines J33s, and two great big, huge 3300, 3350 horsepower engines.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay; and this is a plane that's going to be fighting other airplanes, doing ground support?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Ground support.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. And so it would have been carrying bombs and rockets and stuff like that?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: No. No. No. We don't do that. Surveillance, checking around where everything was at and reporting back, what are -- what we were doing. And now when I was in VP1 -- no, okay, VP22 -- no VP1, when we were -- I can't remember where we were all at. At first we went -- oh, another thing -- I just got checked into the squadron VP1 at Whidbey Island, I just checked in and, bam, off to Vietnam I went. Left her again with six kids, but they did furnish a big, nice, five bedroom house and everything on Whidbey Island. But back I went over there and that was in --

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: And --

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: -- that was in, that was in Tansanouk. That was in Tansanouk. That was in Saigon. I don't know what it's called.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: So you're in Vietnam at Tansanouk and basically these are surveillance jets that we're using to try to keep track of the Viet Congs and the North Vietnamese, so that the commanders could better figure out where to put our troops, where to send our bombers, where to do this and that to fight the war. Approximately how long were you in Vietnam?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Well, I was there three different times, I think. Now, the -- at first I went to -- first I went to Cameron Bay -- no, that was the second. First I went to Ho Chi Minh that was -- what is it called now.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Well, Saigon is now Ho Chi Minh City?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Ho Chi Minh City we lived in a hotel there.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: At that point in time we were calling it Saigon. We hadn't lost that war yet. What would your rank have been?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Chief, Chief then.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: And a Chief in the Navy is like a Master Sergeant in the Army?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Something like that, yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. You were basically one notch underneath the commissioned officers at the point in time you are a Chief, is that correct?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. Do you want to read that?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Read that out loud.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. This is dated December 12th, 1967 Department of the Navy. This is a letter of Commendation. Letter of Commendation to Chief Aviation Machinist Mate Dennis Dean Hatzenbuehler. "From 15 May 1967 to 15 November 1967 you were assigned numerous and varied tasks within the Maintenance Department while this squadron was deployed to Naval Station Sangley Point, Republic of the Philippines and Cam Ranh Bay, Republic of Vietnam. These tasks included Power Plants Branch Chief Petty Officer, Detachment Maintenance Chief, and Night Maintenance Chief. AsPower Plants Branch Chief you were responsible for and directly supervised the organization and construction of shop spaces to fulfill the needs of maintaining the Squadron's SP-2H aircraft. During your assignment to the Squadron's detachment at Cam Ranh Bay, Republic of Vietnam, you accomplished, with a minimum of personnel and under the most austere and adverse conditions, the task of maintaining six aircraft assigned to Market Time operations against enemy infiltration by sea into South Vietnam. This accomplishment was particularly noteworthy due to the lack of organized supply and support facilities at that advanced base. As night maintenance Chief you continued to demonstrate your outstanding leadership abilities in maintaining a high state of aircraft readiness in support of the squadron's mission during around-the-clock operations. I take great pleasure in commending you for your diligent efforts, superior leadership and exceptional accomplishments which contributed so much to this unit's successful operations in Southeast Asia. Signed LC Day."

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: That was my Skipper.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: So what this sounds like, Chief, these would have been working along the coastline trying to make sure that there would not have been small boats of insurgents coming down from the North that would have infiltrated or attacked our Navy. Okay. This is the --

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Squadron.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: This is the unit commendation for Patrol Squadron One and it talks a little bit about what he was doing out there. He's apparently getting tired of talking. He says, "Just read it. Save my tongue a little bit." "For meritorious service from 15 May through 15 November 1967 while conducting radar and visual surveillance of sea areas along the coast of the Republic of Vietnam as part of Operation Market Time. Patrol Squadron One demonstrated a coordinated effort in executing duties as an integral part of the Coastal Surveillance Force, from the initial austere establishment phase at Cam Ranh Bay, Republic of Vietnam through the fully operational phase. Conducting around-the-clock patrols, Patrol Squadron One participated in 479 missions, logging nearly 6,000 hours of combat flight time and averaging over eight hours per sortie for a total 693 sorties. During this period, a total of 75 communist-bloc ships and hundreds of other ships were sighted and photographed, yielding invaluable intelligence information vital to the overall intelligence collection effort in the South China Sea. On 11 July 1967, Patrol Squadron One detected, photographed and identified a North Vietnamese trawler during an infiltration attempt and, along with Market Time surface units, tracked the trawler for four days, leading ultimately to the successful, intact capture of the infiltrating vessel and the denying of tons of arms, ammunition, and supplies to the insurgent Viet Cong. The initiative, versatility, reliability, and professional competence displayed by the officers and men of Patrol Squadron One were in keeping with the highest traditions of the United States Naval Service. All personnel attached to and serving with Patrol Squadron One during the period designated above, or any part thereof, are hereby authorized to wear the Meritorious Unit Commendation Ribbon."

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: That was the second time. That was that friend of yours was killed.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. So --

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Now, you know it all. Now, you know my history.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Three different tours in Vietnam and when did you leave Vietnam the last time?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Oh, okay, yeah.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Yeah. Before your 30 is up you get six months where you're at shore duty to do anything you want to do, go to school for whatever you want to do. I went to school for -- I sent to a bunch of schools and I got a bunch of replys. Dallas called me up in '71 March, I think it was, to see if I wanted to come down and be a postmaster, be a mail carrier. I took an exam for that. Marietta, Ohio called me up, offered me a GS11 and I turned that down. And then another outfit in Ohio called me up, offered me $17,000 a year I'd be a rep and I -- well, I called -- I wrote back and said what more, what does it consist of. Well, on the Islands all the time with these squadrons we have reps out there, tech reps, you've got a problem with this engine you call him up. Well, we have three squadrons out there all the same type airplanes. One rep that knows all these engines, every part of the engine, supposed to know, every time I'd call him I couldn't find him. "He's on the other side." So I'd ask Ron, "No, he hasn't been here all day." This went on all the time. So when they said you be a rep overseas for this biggest airplane they got today, whatever it is, I don't remember, but they showed it on TV the other day. That big sucker flying that's what they wanted me to be. That's -- I turned them down when they said "rep". If they'd have said something else I might have taken it, but out of that, no.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: So when you got done in Vietnam --

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: -- you're nearing the end of your 30?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Right. My six months is up and I'm ready to go home.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. And so your last duty station was where before you left the service? Dennis Hatzenbuehler:: It's not -- oh, my last one was -- well, now, they asked me where I wanted to go. You get your choice of duty. I said, "Okay I want to go back to Hutch and be with my mother and I'll go up to that Reserve base up in Kansas City, Olathe." I got transferred to Olathe with the Reserves. Now, I never been a reserve before. I had no idea what I was going to expect. Now, this is really nice Reserves. They put me in -- the minute I checked in I just wanted -- I'm getting ready to retire. I'm so sick and tired of airplanes and stuff. Well, they put me in charge of all the aviation again. God, I had all them Reserves and I had aircraft so I said, "Well, okay." To make a long story short, to make -- so we had a great big counter. This pilot come in and writing their gripes down. That's how we worked on the airplanes, the pilots filled their gripes out. I had five sailors up there, five Second Class Reserves. All had a stool. They would sit there. And all these five Second Class every one of them had over three degrees. Here I'm a -- flunked kindergarten because they asked me how to spell my mother's name and I spelled it M-O-T-H-E-R and it was Teresa, so they flunked me in kindergarten. These guys had four or five degrees and I'm a little old joker sitting back there, but they were the nicest people and I wouldn't favor the Reserves, although I was Reserve, the minute I got in the service I changed regular Navy. I got out of that Reserve business. Another thing, while I was aboard ship after the war was over there they said, okay, all the Reserves that got so many points you can get out. Well, they didn't say what. They just said, you got so many points. So I waited in line on the hangar deck for half an hour and I got up there. I said, "I got 350 points. I can get out." "Hatzenbuehler", he says, "you're a regular Navy. Get the hell out of here." I forgot I shipped over. But anyway these Reserves were fantastic. Now they closed the base down --

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: In Olathe?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: In Olathe. It was sometime in '69, yeah -- no '70, March of '70 they closed it down. Before then the skipper told me he says, "Chief, we'll transfer you when you sell all these airplanes." I had jets. And I had recips. So I got a hold of Memphis, Tennessee and I think I sent the recips to Memphis. Got a hold of Dallas and they took the jets. I called that Skipper and I said, "I sold your airplanes and I'm leaving." And I left and I went to Corpus Christi, Texas. They said, "We'll send you back to Corpus, because that's where you opened the bank." So you're called a bank owner and go get the picture they showed us retiring. So I retired down there after I, after everything was squared away and so I came back to Pratt and that was it.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. You married Phalba. And you spent right at 30 years in the military?Dennis Hatzenbuehler:: Yeah. Get back to -- it wasn't quite 30 now. An old Chief -- this is when I retired, me and momma. They retired mother the same time they retired me. Now, an old Chief back when I was a kid told me said, "Now, look, boy," he said, "when it comes time to ship over, ship over six months early. That will count as a full year." I said, "Okay." So I did. Every time I come to ship over I shipped six months ahead of time. That let me get out at 29 and a half years and the Navy counted at 30.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Let's talk about that 29 and a half years and we're going to let Phalba correct you on this. In that 29 and a half years how many nights would you and your wife have been, you know, in the same place at the same time in that 29 and a half years?

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: We were together, literally together, three years day and night out of his Navy career.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: And I know that you'd have --

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: When he went to work in the morning and come home that night, three years.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: And I know that there was some leaves and sounds like some of these leaves were pretty darn short. You thought you were going to be home for a month or two and you were just there a few days?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Get back to leave, never took any leave in the Navy. I could hold my leave and sell it when I got ready to ship over and that's how I raised a family. My 30 days leave, I let it build up to so many days and when I shipped over I got paid for that.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: And you and Phalba had how many children?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Six.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. And so for 26 and a half of those 29 and a half years she basically was alone taking care of kids so that you could be taking care of the country and how many, how many medals did they give her?

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Navy wives don't get nothing. Let me tell you something, these Navy wives -- when he was in the Navy overseas and that, we sat at home. We didn't know what was going on. These little girls nowadays they got TV. They've got telephones. They've got all these goodies. They know what their husbands are doing and where they're at, but we never knew anything. We sat there day upon day and if you went and asked somebody in the squadron, oh, my God you were in trouble, because you weren't supposed to ask questions.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. We've come to that September or December 1st, 1970.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: That last salute?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: You're going to be a civilian again?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Where'd you go? What'd you do?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Came back to Pratt.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Come home to take care of momma.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: And you come home to take care of momma?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: My mother, yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: And she lived here in Pratt on North Jackson Street?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: North Jackson.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: All right. And you got a little house not too far from where she was?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Across the street.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: All right. And I know you did some other work before you became the bailiff at the Court. What job did you have to have some money coming in besides your Naval pension when you came to Pratt?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Swept the floors at Gibsons.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay. And then you went from sweeping the floors to the manager and how quick?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Three and a half years.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Three years, yeah, three years. No, I managed it for four years. And to make a long story short, I was up in the office waiting on some guys, buyers or sellers, and salesmen and one of the girls called me up at our office on the 02 deck in the building and where I could see down and see everything and called me up front and said, "Come to the front, please." And so I was with this salesman and I waited about three or four minutes, so then I went up. I figured it was a check to sign or something. And as I was coming up there a guy was coming in and said, "Hi." I said, "Hi." He said, "What's that guy doing here?" I said, "Who?" He said, "That guy getting out of that old Chevy out there." I said, "Well, I have no idea." He said, "That's old Sam Walton." I says, "Who?" He says, "That's Sam Walton." And the little girl at the cash register said, "He wanted to talk to you, but you didn't show up so he left." This was in September, I don't know what day it was. Next morning I went to Ann Braden, my secretary, and said, "Put my resignation in. I'm getting the hell out of here." I knew there was going to be a Wal-mart here in Pratt. Sure enough there was. That's when I went to work -- but that was old Sam Walton. So that's why I got out of there and went to work for -- where'd I go to work for? The Courthouse, who? The Courthouse with you people.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: And Dennis I know that you've done some other things besides -- I know you've been very active in the Catholic Church. You've been active in the Knights of Columbus.
