You were Grand Night of the Knights of Columbus for awhile. You were kind of the business manager for Sacred Heart Catholic Church for a number of years a few years ago. Approximately when were you doing that?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Okay. 1941 when I came back here or 1940 from January --

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: January of 1971. We have elections for different jobs in the church, so I was just new and Father Butler, no, Father Bill Vogel was a friend of my aunt and after mass he was out there all the time. He liked to farm. But anyway my name got on the list. Nobody asked me. Nobody said nothing. My name got on there and I got elected to the finance committee. So in 19 March of '71 I went in the finance committee and I stayed there until sometime in the middle, I want to say -- when did Monsignor die, '82?" I finally said, "Hey, I've had enough." In 1974 Monsignor started the enlisted -- the --

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Lay ministers?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Lay ministers and there was eight of us assigned and so we, we distributed communion and all that stuff to the sick and my mother was up in her 80s going blind and so she liked to go to 7:00 o'clock mass and I took her to every mass. Well, every night for some reason or another for the next, I don't know how many years, Saturday night I had to go distribute communion up there on the altar and I left and it got so that I watched mother coming up the aisle and going to fall. And so I just, I went to Staabs to Anita and told her, she was the boss of things and I kept griping, there was eight of us assigned. Well, I can't remember the guy that worked that was the professor out at the college. He left. That left seven. Somebody else left. That left six. Every Saturday and Sunday night the same and I kept going to the people and saying, "Hey, why can't we get some help here?" I mean, every Saturday night and I didn't mind it except for my mother. I would have still been there if it hadn't been for mother. I saw one night that she had no idea where she was at and so I just said, "Hey, I've got to pull the plug." And then they finally started getting other people on there. I done that for eight years and -- but, no, I enjoyed, I enjoyed my work.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: When?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: The Bishop asked me, the Bishop asked me, of course, Bishop Gerber and the Bishop were, you know, and so Marvin came to me and said, "The Bishop asked me to ask you if you would stay what you're doing till they get a new Priest." And I said, "Sure." So one night about 10:00 o'clock at night the phone rang and I answered it. "This is Bishop Gerber. Is this Dennis?" "Yes, Bishop." And I didn't know what to say. I said, "Yes Bishop." And "I want to see you." And I'll be there at a certain time and he said, "I want you to have some men there." And I said, "Okay." I picked the people that was on the committee with me. And so which I think was Penka and Henderson, somebody else. So we discussed what we wanted and then about two or three weeks, four weeks he called me up again and said, "Hey, I want to talk to you again." Wanted to know what kind of Priest we wanted. So I said "Well, we'll take a Priest that don't worry about money." Well, we got a Priest without money.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: That was Father Pottorff. You know who that guy -- who that other one was that was in on that meeting?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: You?

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Okay. I can't remember. I knew it was -- I knew it was somebody, but I didn't know if there was three or four of them.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: We sat there in the rectory, visited with the Bishop and said, "You send us a spiritual leader. We'll take care of everything else." And --

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: That's right. Now, you're right. I didn't remember. All that I knew there was something about that, but I didn't know. You know, but it was nice. It was nice. I enjoyed Father Zenner Monsignor Zenner. I loved him. Sometimes we fought, remember, over the pew deal.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Oh, yeah. He wanted to sign a contract that didn't have a price in it and young lawyer Bob wouldn't let him do it. That made him mad.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: I was President of the Parrish Council. So I turned it to Bob Blasi. I had a bunch of good people that I could talk to that was why it was so nice. I had the people there. Same with the Knights. When I was Grand Knight for two years I had a good committee to do the work. I didn't. They did all the work.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Chief, let's, let's start wrapping this up. The Veterans History Project is probably more worried about the military stuff than they are some of the background stuff, but I think it's fine that we need to understand that Veterans are more than soldiers and sailors. They're human beings. They have family. They have families. They have a life beyond the military and if we want them to be at their absolute peek for their military service we have to make sure that their family is taken care of and that other aspects of their lives are taken care of. My son is a Senior in high school. I don't think he has any interest in a military career, but if he grabbed you at the back of church sometime in the next couple of weeks and said, "I'm looking into the service." What would you say to him?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: I would say go. You know, it's up to him. If he wants to go, that's fine. All I tell them is if you can say, "Yes, sir or no, sir, go. If you can't say yes, sir or no, sir" --

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: If you can take orders.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: If you can't say yes or no, don't go. You know, I had three of my girls that worked for me at the Gibsons had sons, all of them come to see me. Today they all done their 30 years in. All made the highest you can make in the enlisted ranks. I don't know how many people I've talked to back in the '70s that joined the service and now they're all retired and they went to their max of --

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: You also have a job security. That's the main thing. The job security in the service.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Oh, there's so many people that are hurt now.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: When he was in the service friends of our's were losing their jobs. He didn't. Uh-uh. What I'm trying to say that's the thing, orders and job security.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Well, I had six kids. Now, I was to get out in '46 and I called mother up and I said, "Mother I'm thinking about getting out." She said, "Dennis, the cars on east and west 54 are bumper to bumper. I'd stay in." So I did. I was going to get out in '46. I just had enough of that stuff. But anyway then it came time to ship over, I kept thinking of the kids and --

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: See at the last there we had a bunch of girls in the high school.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: We've had Dennis' wife of 65 years, Phalba has been participating in some of this. I don't know that -- I don't think there's a spot for the Veteran's wife to sign the release form. We're going to go ahead and send it in. But Phalba do you want to add anything about what it was like having your husband off on the carrier and you're taking care of the babies and you don't hear very much and what was it like raising a family while your husband was off at war?

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: I didn't know any different, anything different. I was born in the service and when I married a serviceman that was it. That was what I was supposed to do. I didn't like it sometimes.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: If I'd have married one of these girls here in Pratt they would have never lasted with me.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Our girls, they wouldn't have anything to do with a serviceman and Junior ...

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: He said, "I've had enough of us transferring back and forth." He said, "I want no part of this."

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: But it's a rough life. But you have to learn to cope with it.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: My brother-in-law, I guess, is going to get a Navy man in the family. My wife's brother's daughter is the one that's been in all the Miss Kansas Pageants accepted a proposal from a fella that's graduating from Annapolis this spring and he's heading for flight school and I might have to bring her by and let her visit so she understands what it's like to be married to a Naval aviator?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Things have changed so much now.

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: It's like I say, now the girls have got a snap. They don't realize. They're griping, but they've got a snap.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Now, you get --

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: You know, he was in South America. I was pregnant and I was supposed to go, you know, you go to the dispensary of the hospital on the base to be taken care of. You know, what they told me? We can't handle you anymore. Your husband is in South America. I went home and we lived in the woods in back (Zephyr) out in the boonies. I had no medication. No doctor. Nothing. Until I go to San Diego and Phalba was born in July. We went there in June. And that's the first time I saw a doctor. But they refused and nowadays they don't do that to the girls.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: See, it's altogether different now. It's a pleasure to be in these services now. I mean, you've got everything. When I got transferred from the east to the West Coast they give me five days to get across country. Couple of days a year. Now, they give you half a year and just hand you full of money and say, go. Them days, man ...

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: It's up to the individual. You got to have alot of stamina and alot of faith and alot of guts. You do. That's the whole thing.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Chief, you mentioned that somebody that's going to be in the service has to be able to take orders. In any organization you get folks who abuse their power. In the service the folks that abuse their power, does the service grind them out and get rid of them?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Depends on what it is. Yeah, or they can go to the brig and spend six months in the brig. People don't do that in the civilian life. They fire you and that's it. In the service ...

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: The system works that the folks who are, who are in it for the wrong reason -- I'll use police officers as an example. We have alot of turnover with police officers. Some of them are there for the wrong reasons. They're there because they like the power. They like having the gun on their hips. They like the ability to boss folks around and abuse them and generally within a year or two we get rid of those guys. I'm assuming the guy that goes into the Navy with the idea, or goes into any branch of the service with the idea that I'm going to be a boss and I'm going to boss people around and I'm going to be, I mean, they don't think they're going to be abusive, but they're in it for the power trip, the system works that we get rid of them.

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: You get rid of them in the Navy. You see you have to -- you get performance tests every month or every quarter, you get a performance test on you. And when it comes time to enlist if that's not up to par ... say, if that's, let's see, we're marking 4, if that's a 2.8 you're not going to be enlisted. 1959 they had money shortages and so they kicked out all the Chiefs that had so much time and got rid of them regardless of their performance. I was one of the lucky ones. I didn't have -- alot of people didn't get to finish 30. I got to finish 30, but you just had to, you know, there was alot of them didn't get to finish 30.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Chief, I'm going to ask you a couple of quick questions that if you got a answer for it, great. If you don't that's fine, too. As far -- and I know that you said meeting Phalba was the best day you were in the Navy. But leaving the family out of it, 30-year career, what was the best day, what was the worst day, of those 30 years?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Well, the best day was the day I retired. And the worst day was, I think, was when we got, we took two crash drives, one right after the other and I still was walking around when alot of my buddies was gone. I thought that was -- it was a good day when I pulled into Hunters Point with the ship.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: When you took those two Kamikazes did you think the ship was going down?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: You know, we never thought of that. You never thought. You had a job to do and you did it. You know, it was funny, the aircraft carrier was on fire. People were screaming, running around. You were just trying to do a job. If you saw a guy sitting over there that needed help you went and helped him. Nothing else went through your mind. I guess it was survival. I don't know, but I didn't think of that. I just wanted to help somebody and that was it all the time we got hit. Now, one time we were pinned in a little room and, boy, the old deck, we had heavy shoes on. The old deck was getting hot. I mean, it was getting warm. We had a port hole over here. The Missouri was in back of us, just real close. We could throw a candy bar and hit the bow. As I was going out the window and I was climbing out they dropped a monkey-line, what they call a monkey-line. There was three, or four of us in there. We hadn't got -- flames everywhere, so we went through this port hole. There was two parachutes coming down and the Missouri boy sitting over there let them go. As I was climbing -- now, I wasn't -- I just saw them people.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: You say he "let them go", they shot them?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Yeah. So we just went up, but I know they were limp coming down because we heard by scuttlebutt, or something, that the Missouri got in trouble over there. But, you know, I wasn't -- I never got scared or nothing. I just, just, you just done it. I mean, flying.Robert Schmisseur:: When you knew the ship wasn't going down, you know, the immediate danger is over, the fires are out, got your steam back up, you're, you know, you're going and you think about your friends that got killed. You think about your friends that got the living daylights, you know, you talk about your friend lost his arm. I know you got a leg messed up in that battle. You had a broken ankle, didn't you? That was when the deck folded up around you?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Sit down and cry. No?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: No. No. I remember her dad came down and looked at it and ordered a guy to -- my toes were getting all blue and puffing out and he got a coreman to cut the relief off.Robert Schmisseur:: They had it bound up too tight?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: But anyway but, you know, I never thought about -- after it was over with we was just worrying about where's our -- we're worrying about the next flight, but, of course, we knew we couldn't fly. Where we going? Are we getting to go back to the States already? Or one time we got hit we thought we'd come back to the States, but we pulled up to a big old repair ship and we stayed there for 30 days while they came aboard. Outside of that, all the time we were hit I was up on the flight deck watching the airplanes. I don't know, it wasn't very bright, I guess, but anyway now -- there was only a couple of us during that kind of stuff to get up on the flight deck. I could. But anyway there was a few of us that could, but generally when we was squirming I stayed down on the cat walk and somewhere where I could see what was going on, so I could make a move.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Chief, anything else you went to tell the Veterans History Project?

sp.speaker: Dennis Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: No. I think I've talked enough.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: Phalba, anything else you want to say?

sp.speaker: Phalba Hatzenbuehler
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Robert Schmisseur
sp.p: I was not in the military. But I appreciate that I get to live in a free country and I get to have my family in a free country, because other people stood up and served. When I finished high school my draft number was 113. It was the height of the Vietnam War and I wanted to go to college rather than 16 weeks later be in Vietnam. So I took the deferment and by the time my, by the time I'd finished with college we were coming out of Vietnam and the numbers were being reduced and so I didn't get called to serve. But I very much appreciate those that did and it, it's a shame that we didn't have some of the parades, you know, we had the ticker tape parades at the end of World War II. We didn't do it for the men and women that fought in Vietnam. We didn't really do it as it relates to alot of the conflicts since then. But on behalf of the United States of America, thank you for your service. And I appreciate the folks that stood at home so that these guys could serve in the military and God bless both of you. I love you both.
